forces.title: UK Industrial Energy Prices Undermine Sector Competitiveness
forces.description: Industrial energy prices in the UK are approximately 75% higher than the G7 average, severely eroding the competitiveness of energy-intensive industries. This price disparity increases the risk of deindustrialisation and the offshoring of emissions, indirectly impacting demand for domestically produced oil and gas as industrial activity contracts and energy-intensive sectors struggle to compete. Such an environment creates a challenging demand backdrop for UK E&P, pushing investment and production elsewhere.

forces.title: Elevated Oil and Gas Prices Due to Global Geopolitical Uncertainty
forces.description: Oil and gas prices remain elevated compared to historical averages, driven by persistent geopolitical uncertainty, particularly from the Middle East conflict. This situation creates a tailwind for larger oil and gas producers in the UK, benefiting from higher commodity prices and enabling them to maintain stronger balance sheets and sustain investment in E&P. However, volatility and the risk of price corrections remain significant, requiring careful monitoring of commodity exposure and liquidity.

forces.title: Intensifying Global Geopolitical Instability Disrupts Energy Supply Chains
forces.description: Escalating tensions, particularly in the Middle East and Red Sea, have significantly tightened global energy markets, increasing risk and driving up commodity prices. The Strait of Hormuz crisis and pipeline disruptions highlight critical vulnerabilities in global oil and gas supply routes, leading to persistent volatility and elevated risk premia. For UK E&P, this translates to both potential price benefits but also heightened operational risks and cost inflation across supply chains, demanding robust resilience measures.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: LNG Buyers Prioritize Security of Supply Over Cost Minimization
forces.description: In the wake of transit disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, LNG buyers are undergoing a structural shift in procurement strategies, prioritizing security of supply over traditional cost minimization. Around 80% of buyers expect significant changes, with geographic diversification emerging as the top priority. This implies a willingness to pay a premium for reliable, diversified supply, creating opportunities for non-Middle East gas producers, including potential benefits for UK natural gas E&P.
forces.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement

forces.title: Global Push for Geographic Diversification in LNG Supply
forces.description: Geographic diversification of LNG supply has become a top priority for buyers globally, with nearly all respondents in Asia and Europe planning to increase suppliers and diversify sourcing in the next 2-3 years. This strategic shift is driven by a desire to combat supply disruption risks, as evidenced by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. This creates a significant opportunity for non-traditional LNG suppliers, potentially benefiting UK natural gas E&P by increasing demand for non-Gulf sources.
forces.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement

forces.title: UK and Norway Discussing New Oil and Gas Capacity Amidst Security Needs
forces.description: Amidst global energy security concerns, both Norway and the United Kingdom are reportedly discussing the development of new oil and gas capacity. This indicates a recognition of the strategic importance of domestic production to reduce reliance on volatile international markets and imports. For UK E&P, such discussions could translate into supportive policy frameworks and investment opportunities, potentially reversing the trend of declining domestic production and enhancing national energy resilience.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: UKCS Investment Trajectory Hinges on Policy and Regulatory Choices
forces.description: The future of investment in the UK Continental Shelf (UKCS) is fundamentally shaped by prevailing policy and regulatory choices, not solely geological potential. OEUK emphasizes that while vast resources exist, current fiscal and regulatory environments have constrained the pipeline of future developments. This structural dependence on policy means that government decisions are critical in determining whether significant opportunities for strengthening domestic production, supporting investment, and sustaining infrastructure are realized or missed.

forces.title: Cost Inflation Impacts Offshore Energy Supply Chains in UK
forces.description: The war in the Middle East has driven up commodity prices and inflation globally, with cost inflation directly hitting offshore energy supply chains in the UK. This increases operating expenses for E&P companies, impacting profitability and potentially deferring investment decisions. While elevated commodity prices can offer some offset, persistent cost pressures add a significant headwind, requiring companies to manage supply chain resilience and operational efficiency rigorously.

forces.title: Fiscal Reform and Pragmatic Licensing Could Unlock UKCS Investment
forces.description: A more competitive fiscal regime from 2027 and a pragmatic approach to licensing are identified as critical drivers to unlock significant investment in the UKCS. OEUK's modelling suggests this could enable 111 additional projects, attracting £50 billion in private capital and producing 3.25 billion boe. Such reforms would sustain domestic output, reduce future import dependence, and materially improve the long-term energy security, cost, and emissions profile of the UK.

forces.title: UK Government Ban on New Exploration Licenses Stifles Activity
forces.description: The UK government's ban on new exploration licenses has directly contributed to record-low well activity, with no exploration wells drilled in the UK for the first time since production began. This policy decision acts as a significant headwind, preventing the replenishment of reserves and accelerating the decline of domestic oil and gas production, contrasting sharply with Norway's active licensing rounds and sustained production levels. It fundamentally undermines long-term investment in UK E&P.

forces.title: Record-Low Well Activity Signals UKCS Decline Without Policy Change
forces.description: Well activity in the UK Continental Shelf (UKCS) has plummeted to record lows, marked by the absence of a single exploration well drilled in the UK in the past year. This stark decline, coupled with the UK government's ban on new licenses, signals an accelerating natural decline in domestic production. Without significant policy and fiscal changes to encourage investment, this trend will lead to further degradation of production forecasts and increased reliance on imports.

forces.title: Current Fiscal and Regulatory Regimes Constrain UKCS Development Pipeline
forces.description: The current fiscal and regulatory regimes in the UK are severely constraining the pipeline of future oil and gas developments in the UKCS. This environment has deterred investment, leading to consistent downgrades in production outlooks by the NSTA and pushing capital overseas to competing basins. Without a stable and competitive long-term investment framework, declining activity levels and weaker production forecasts are expected to continue, compromising future domestic supply.

forces.title: Global Energy Demand Growth Slowed, Impacting Commodity Markets
forces.description: Global energy demand growth slowed to 1.3% in 2025, primarily reflecting weaker global economic growth and continued improvements in energy efficiency. This slowdown can translate into moderated demand for oil and gas, influencing commodity prices and creating a more challenging market for E&P companies. While geopolitical events can cause temporary spikes, underlying demand trends set the broader context for investment and production strategies.

forces.title: Coal Substitution Offsets Gas Demand Growth in Asia
forces.description: Rising LNG prices and supply uncertainty, particularly due to the Middle East conflict, have prompted several Asian economies to increase coal-fired generation to ensure energy security and manage consumer costs. This fuel switching has resulted in weaker gas demand in parts of Asia, offsetting what would otherwise have been stronger growth in global natural gas consumption. This trend acts as a headwind for global gas E&P, potentially limiting export opportunities for UK gas producers.

forces.title: Natural Gas Critical for UK Electricity System Balancing
forces.description: Natural gas continues to play a critical and indispensable role in balancing the UK's electricity system, especially during periods of low renewable output, seasonal demand peaks, and wider system stress. Despite expanding renewable power generation, the need for flexible and dispatchable energy supply ensures sustained demand for natural gas. This fundamental requirement for grid stability provides a strong, structural tailwind for UK natural gas E&P.

forces.title: Declining Domestic Production Impairs UK Midstream Infrastructure Viability
forces.description: A decline in domestic oil and gas production in the UKCS directly impacts the viability of critical midstream infrastructure such as pipelines, processing facilities, and terminals. Lower production volumes reduce infrastructure utilization, increasing the marginal cost of throughput and placing pressure on asset economics. This creates a self-reinforcing cycle where weakened infrastructure viability further accelerates rationalization, posing a significant challenge not just for midstream operators but also for the long-term prospects of UK E&P.

forces.title: AI Adoption Enhances Operational Efficiency in Upstream Oil and Gas
forces.description: The adoption of AI and data science tools is emerging as a significant upside driver for upstream oil and gas operators. AI-enabled diagnostics can unlock the full potential of mature offshore assets, improving forecasting of well production, optimizing marine logistics, and enhancing equipment maintenance. These advancements lead to measurable productivity gains, reduced non-productive drilling time, and improved asset care, creating opportunities for substantial operational improvements and value creation in E&P.
forces.source_title: AI in Energy: From Pilots to Payoff

forces.title: Fossil Fuels and Renewables Grow in Parallel, Delaying Peak Oil Demand
forces.description: Contrary to some energy transition narratives, the global energy system is experiencing parallel growth across both fossil fuels and renewables, delaying the long-predicted 'peak' for fossil fuels. In 2025, global oil demand increased by 1.3 mbpd, and fossil fuels added more energy in absolute terms than solar and wind. This structural dynamic indicates sustained global demand for oil and gas, requiring E&P companies to continue investing to meet growing energy needs alongside renewable expansion.
forces.source_title: Investing in the energy transition: Time to look at whole-system value

viewpoints.title: Larger UK Oil & Gas Producers Positioned for Resilience Amidst Energy Transition
viewpoints.description: Allianz UK's Sector Head for Energy, Nicole White, highlights a widening divide within the UK energy sector. Larger oil and gas producers, alongside renewable energy companies, are expected to benefit from elevated commodity prices and possess stronger balance sheets. This financial strength allows them to absorb ongoing market volatility and sustain investment required for the energy transition. In contrast, smaller players, especially retail suppliers, face higher risks and have less capacity to manage further cost shocks, suggesting a more challenging outlook for subscale operators.

viewpoints.title: Global Energy System Proves Resilient to Major Supply Disruptions So Far
viewpoints.description: McKinsey states that the global energy system has demonstrated unexpected resilience in the face of the significant Strait of Hormuz crisis of 2026, the largest modern energy supply disruption. This resilience is attributed to existing shock absorbers like strategic petroleum reserves and bypass pipelines. While the impact has been cushioned by these measures, and global growth has slowed but remained positive, the uneven burden of the shock and thinning inventories indicate lingering vulnerabilities and potential long-term energy security concerns.
viewpoints.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

viewpoints.title: UK Continental Shelf Future Dependent on Policy, Not Geology Alone
viewpoints.description: Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) asserts that the future trajectory of the UK Continental Shelf (UKCS) is not predetermined by its mature geology. The North Sea still holds significant untapped resources, but their recovery hinges on political and regulatory decisions. The report emphasizes that a failure to invest in domestic resources will lead to increased reliance on energy imports. OEUK advocates for policy choices that strengthen domestic production, support investment, and sustain critical infrastructure to reduce import dependence and leverage existing geological potential.

viewpoints.title: Domestic Energy Production is Crucial for UK Economic and Security Resilience
viewpoints.description: OEUK highlights that domestic energy production is a cornerstone of UK economic resilience and national security, especially in an increasingly volatile world. With the UK currently relying on imports for over 40% of its energy, home-grown supplies underpin manufacturing competitiveness, support strategic industries, and provide essential feedstocks. The report argues that prioritizing domestic energy reduces exposure to geopolitical instability, strengthens the balance of payments, safeguards jobs, and ensures long-term energy resilience.

viewpoints.title: UK Oil and Gas Production Stability is Fragile Without New Investment
viewpoints.description: OEUK reports that UK oil and gas production remained relatively stable between 2025 and 2026, offering a stronger near-term outlook than many had anticipated. However, this stability is identified as fragile, largely driven by project delays, revised development schedules, and asset life extensions, rather than a new wave of sanctioned investment. The report warns that the pipeline of future developments remains severely constrained by the current fiscal and regulatory regimes, leading to a cautious outlook despite short-term stability.

viewpoints.title: NSTA Production Forecast Downgrades Reflect Investor Confidence, Not Geology
viewpoints.description: OEUK contends that the National Gas Transmission System (NSTA)'s consistent downgrading of UKCS production outlooks and total resource recovery projections stems from waning investor confidence due to the fiscal and political environment, rather than a reassessment of the basin's geological potential. The report argues that significant remaining resources still exist in the North Sea, and the opportunities identified in 2019 are still valid today. OEUK's modelling suggests that with appropriate fiscal and regulatory reforms, these opportunities could be unlocked.

viewpoints.title: Global Energy System Grows Across All Fuels, Fossil Fuel Peak Elusive
viewpoints.description: McKinsey’s analysis suggests that the long-predicted 'peak' for fossil fuels remains elusive, as the global energy system continues to grow across all fuel types to meet ever-increasing demand. In 2025, both fossil fuels and renewables saw growth, with fossil fuels adding more energy in absolute terms. The report emphasizes that the system is not replacing one fuel type with another, but rather building all fuel and power industries in parallel, challenging common assumptions about the energy transition.
viewpoints.source_title: Investing in the energy transition: Time to look at whole-system value

viewpoints.title: Natural Gas Remains Structural Fuel for Decades in Many Geographies
viewpoints.description: McKinsey asserts that natural gas is considered a structural fuel expected to remain an important component of the energy system in many geographies for decades to come. This view challenges the 'bridge fuel' assumption, indicating that gas will maintain a significant role beyond a transitional period. This perspective suggests continued demand and relevance for natural gas upstream operations, particularly in regions where it supports system reliability and meets growing electricity needs.
viewpoints.source_title: Investing in the energy transition: Time to look at whole-system value

market_sizing.methodology: Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) reports the UK's offshore energy sector contributes £36.7 billion in economic value (GVA) annually and supports approximately 245,000 jobs. This figure represents the total GVA from the offshore energy sector, of which oil and gas upstream activities form a significant component.

demand_drivers.description: Fossil fuels provided 74% of the UK's inland energy consumption in 2025, indicating continued high demand for oil and gas.

market_sizing.methodology: In 2025, fossil fuels accounted for 74% of inland energy consumption in the UK. This highlights the country's heavy reliance on oil and gas despite efforts toward energy transition, underscoring their continued importance in the overall energy mix.

demand_drivers.description: Widening gap between domestic production and demand leads to increased imports of oil, gas, and electricity.

market_sizing.methodology: The UK's net spend on imported oil, gas, and electricity totaled £84 billion in 2025, representing approximately 2.8% of the country's GDP. This figure underscores the UK's increasing reliance on international energy markets and the significant economic value transferred overseas due to declining domestic production.

UK oil and gas production levels fell to 1.1 million boe per day (mbpd) in 2025, a significant decline of 75% from its peak of 4.5 mbpd in 1999. The NSTA's current projection for total resource recovery from the UKCS between 2025 and 2050 stands at 3.8 billion boe, further highlighting the basin's decline under current conditions, with a forecast of 0.6 mbpd by 2030.

demand_drivers.description: Total UK natural gas requirement projected for the 2025-2035 period, driven by continued energy needs.

market_sizing.methodology: The UK is estimated to require 561 billion cubic meters (bcm) of natural gas over the period 2025-2035. Under current NSTA production projections, the UK is expected to produce only 176 bcm during this decade. However, OEUK's 'Upside Potential' scenario, driven by an investable fiscal regime and pragmatic licensing, could increase domestic production to 288 bcm for the same period, bringing the total potential gas production for 2025-2050 to 456 bcm.

pnl_drivers.description: Fiscal reform and licensing approach can unlock significant private investment.

new_opportunities.description: 111 additional projects could produce 3.25 billion boe, sustaining output and reducing import dependency.

market_sizing.methodology: OEUK's modelling indicates that fiscal reform and a renewed approach to licensing from 2027 could unlock 111 additional projects in the UKCS, attracting £50 billion in private capital investment. These projects have the potential to produce an additional 3.25 billion boe, almost doubling the UKCS' output over the next 25 years and maintaining production levels around 1 million boe per day into the 2030s.

pnl_drivers.description: Tax receipts are highly influenced by commodity prices, production volumes, and investment activity in the UKCS.

market_sizing.methodology: The UKCS offshore oil and gas sector contributed £4.5 billion in net tax revenues to the UK government in the 2024/25 fiscal year. Historically, the sector has generated nearly £500 billion in cumulative tax receipts (real terms) since the early 1960s, averaging over £10 billion per year since 1980/81. This highlights its significant and ongoing fiscal value.

demand_drivers.description: Overall energy demand growth, including oil, continues to drive significant capital expenditure in upstream oil.

market_sizing.methodology: Global investment in the upstream oil sector reached approximately $540 billion in 2025, making it the largest fossil-fuel capital expenditure category. This figure represents nearly half of the total investment directed towards fossil fuels, power generation, and low-carbon technologies globally, indicating substantial ongoing capital deployment in oil exploration and production worldwide.
market_sizing.source_title: Investing in the energy transition: Time to look at whole-system value

demand_drivers.description: Factors like increased cooling demand in Asia, expansion in freight and petrochemicals, significant data center growth, and industrial capacity expansion due to reshoring drove oil demand.

market_sizing.methodology: Global oil demand increased by approximately 1.3 million barrels per day (mbpd) in 2025, representing an acceleration from the growth rates observed in 2023–24. This growth contributed to an overall increase of 4.5 exajoules in fossil fuel demand in 2025, challenging expectations that oil demand would peak before 2030 and indicating robust global consumption.
market_sizing.source_title: Investing in the energy transition: Time to look at whole-system value

market_sizing.methodology: In Q4 2025, approximately 21 million barrels per day (mbpd) of oil, comprising 16 mbpd of crude and 5 mbpd of refined products, flowed through the Strait of Hormuz. This critical chokepoint handles roughly 20% of global oil supplies, making its disruption in 2026 a major event for global energy markets.
market_sizing.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis
